oad that registers an `IValidateOptions<TOptions>` implementation by type ([dotnet/runtime #127264](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/127264)). Until this preview, callers had to either inline validation logic in a `Validate(...)` lambda or wire the `IValidateOptions<T>` service up themselves. The new overload lets configuration code register a typed validator the same way it registers any other DI service, and the validator is resolved from the DI container so it can take its own constructor dependencies.

using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;

services.AddOptions<SmtpSettings\>()
    .Configure(s \=> { /\* bind from configuration \*/ })
    .Validate<SmtpSettingsValidator\>();

public sealed class SmtpSettingsValidator : IValidateOptions<SmtpSettings\>
{
    public ValidateOptionsResult Validate(string? name, SmtpSettings options) \=>
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Host)
            ? ValidateOptionsResult.Fail("Host is required.")
            : ValidateOptionsResult.Success;
}

Validation runs the first time `IOptions<TOptions>.Value` is requested and throws `OptionsValidationException` on failure.

## Breaking changes

[](#breaking-changes)

*   Custom `Type` subclasses must override `Type.GetNullableUnderlyingType()` if they support nullable type inspection. The base implementation throws `NotSupportedException` ([dotnet/runtime #126905](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/126905)).
*   The pipe used by the `System.IO.Pipes` shared server has stricter permissions ([dotnet/runtime #127239](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/127239)). Applications that depend on out-of-process access to that implementation detail should review their assumptions.

Thank you [@aw0lid](https://github.com/aw0lid)!

Thank you [@unsafePtr](https://github.com/unsafePtr)!

## Generic GetTypeInfo for System.Text.Json

[](#generic-gettypeinfo-for-systemtextjson)

A common pattern when working with `System.Text.Json` type metadata is to retrieve a `JsonTypeInfo<T>` from `JsonSerializerOptions`, which previously required a manual downcast from the non-generic `GetTypeInfo(Type)` method ([dotnet/runtime#118468](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/118468)). New generic `GetTypeInfo<T>()` and `TryGetTypeInfo<T>()` methods on `JsonSerializerOptions` eliminate this cast and return strongly-typed metadata directly ([dotnet/runtime#123940](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/123940)).

// Before: manual downcast required
JsonTypeInfo<MyType\> info \= (JsonTypeInfo<MyType\>)options.GetTypeInfo(typeof(MyType));

// After: generic method returns the right type directly
JsonTypeInfo<MyType\> info \= options.GetTypeInfo<MyType\>();

// TryGetTypeInfo variant for cases where the type may not be registered
if (options.TryGetTypeInfo<MyType\>(out JsonTypeInfo<MyType\>? typeInfo))
{
    // Use typeInfo
}

This is particularly useful when working with source generation, NativeAOT, and polymorphic serialization scenarios where type metadata access is common.

## Tar Archive Format Selection

[](#tar-archive-format-selection)

New overloads on `TarFile.CreateFromDirectory` accept a `TarEntryFormat` parameter, giving you direct control over the archive format ([dotnet/runtime#123407](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/123407)). The new overloads support all four tar formats — Pax, Ustar, GNU, and V7 — for compatibility with specific tools and environments ([dotnet/runtime#121819](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/121819)).

// Create a GNU format tar archive for Linux compatibility
TarFile.CreateFromDirectory("/source/dir", "/dest/archive.tar",
    includeBaseDirectory: true, TarEntryFormat.Gnu);

// Create a Ustar format archive for broader compatibility
TarFile.CreateFromDirectory("/source/dir", outputStream,
    includeBaseDirectory: false, TarEntryFormat.Ustar);

// Async version
await TarFile.CreateFromDirectoryAsync("/source/dir", "/dest/archive.tar",
    includeBaseDirectory: true, TarEntryFormat.Pax, cancellationToken);

Contents of https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/whats-new/dotnet-11/libraries:
This article describes new features in the .NET libraries for .NET 11. It was last updated for Preview 5.

## Diagnostics and process execution

*   [Process API expansion](#process-api-expansion)
*   [Console FORCE\_COLOR support](#console-force_color-support)

### Process API expansion

[Process](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process) has a substantial set of new APIs that cover common scenarios where you previously had to wire up [OutputDataReceived](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.outputdatareceived#system-diagnostics-process-outputdatareceived)/[ErrorDataReceived](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.errordatareceived#system-diagnostics-process-errordatareceived) events manually or use P/Invoke.

#### Run-and-capture helpers

New one-shot APIs let you launch a process and get its result without manual setup:

```
// One-shot capture: stdout and stderr together, plus exit code.
ProcessTextOutput result = await Process.RunAndCaptureTextAsync(
    "git", ["status", "--porcelain"]);

Console.WriteLine(result.StandardOutput);
Console.WriteLine($"Exit code: {result.ExitStatus.ExitCode}");
```

The full set of helpers includes:

*   [Process.Run](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.run) and [Process.RunAsync](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.runasync) — launch a process and return an exit-status result.
*   [Process.RunAndCaptureText](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.runandcapturetext) and [Process.RunAndCaptureTextAsync](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.runandcapturetextasync) — launch and capture stdout/stderr together with exit code.
*   [Process.ReadAllText(Nullable<TimeSpan>)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.readalltext#system-diagnostics-process-readalltext\(system-nullable\(\(system-timespan\)\)\)), [Process.ReadAllBytes(Nullable<TimeSpan>)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.readallbytes#system-diagnostics-process-readallbytes\(system-nullable\(\(system-timespan\)\)\)), and their async variants — read a child process's standard output in a single call.
*   [Process.ReadAllLines(Nullable<TimeSpan>)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.readalllines#system-diagnostics-process-readalllines\(system-nullable\(\(system-timespan\)\)\)) — synchronously reads all lines of output from a child process, returning a sequence of [ProcessOutputLine](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processoutputline) values that distinguish stdout from stderr.
*   [Process.ReadAllLinesAsync(CancellationToken)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.readalllinesasync#system-diagnostics-process-readalllinesasync\(system-threading-cancellationtoken\)) — returns a stream of [ProcessOutputLine](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processoutputline) values that distinguish stdout from stderr without string parsing.

#### Fire-and-forget launches

*   [Process.StartAndForget](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process.startandforget) — starts a child process when you don't intend to wait for it; the runtime detaches the handle automatically.
*   [ProcessStartInfo.StartDetached](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processstartinfo.startdetached#system-diagnostics-processstartinfo-startdetached) — detaches from the parent's session/console so the child can outlive a terminal exit.
*   [ProcessStartInfo.KillOnParentExit](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.processstartinfo.killonparentexit#system-diagnostics-processstartinfo-killonparentexit) (Windows only) — the child is terminated when the parent process exits.

#### SafeProcessHandle lifecycle methods

[SafeProcessHandle](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle) gains lifecycle methods for advanced scenarios:

*   [SafeProcessHandle.Start(ProcessStartInfo)](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.start#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-start\(system-diagnostics-processstartinfo\)) and a new [SafeProcessHandle.ProcessId](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.processid#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-processid) property — launch and identify processes without going through [Process](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.process) itself.
*   [SafeProcessHandle.Kill()](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.kill#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-kill) and [SafeProcessHandle.Signal(PosixSignal)](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.signal#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-signal\(system-runtime-interopservices-posixsignal\)) — terminate or signal a process by handle.
*   [SafeProcessHandle.WaitForExit()](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.waitforexit#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-waitforexit) and [SafeProcessHandle.WaitForExitAsync(CancellationToken)](/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.win32.safehandles.safeprocesshandle.waitforexitasync#microsoft-win32-safehandles-safeprocesshandle-waitforexitasync\(system-threading-cancellationtoken\)) — wait for a process to exit by handle.

### TLS handshake hardening

Two [System.Net.Security](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.security) items improve TLS (Transport Layer Security) reliability:

*   [SslStream](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.security.sslstream) server-side handshake bounds-checking fixes in `TlsFrameHelper` close several edge cases that could surface as `IOException` on malformed ClientHello records.
*   On Linux, certificate-validation failures now surface as standard TLS alerts to the peer, matching Windows behavior. Connecting clients receive an actionable handshake error instead of a connection drop.

### HTTP/2 automatic downgrade for Windows authentication

[HttpClient](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclient) automatically downgrades to HTTP/1.1 when a request requires Windows authentication (NTLM/Negotiate) over HTTP/2. The HTTP/2 specification disallows the connection-bound authentication schemes that NTLM and Kerberos rely on, so these requests previously failed. With the downgrade in place, applications targeting mixed-authentication environments—common in enterprise intranets—work without explicit `HttpRequestMessage.Version` overrides.

### QUIC stream priority

[QuicStream](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.quic.quicstream) gains a [QuicStream.Priority](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.quic.quicstream.priority#system-net-quic-quicstream-priority) property and a [QuicStream.DefaultPriority](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.quic.quicstream.defaultpriority#system-net-quic-quicstream-defaultpriority) constant that exposes HTTP/3 stream prioritization (RFC 9218). Priority values range from 0 (highest) to 255 (lowest), with a default of 127:

```
// Increase priority for interactive streams
stream.Priority = 64; // Higher priority than the default 127
```

*   `MediaTypeNames.Video.Mpeg` — `"video/mpeg"`
*   `MediaTypeNames.Video.Ogg` — `"video/ogg"`
*   `MediaTypeNames.Video.QuickTime` — `"video/quicktime"`
*   `MediaTypeNames.Video.WebM` — `"video/webm"`

These join the existing `MediaTypeNames.Application`, `MediaTypeNames.Image`, `MediaTypeNames.Text`, and `MediaTypeNames.Multipart` classes.

## Unsafe API accessibility

.NET 11 removes the `[RequiresUnsafe]` attribute from a large set of APIs that take pointer parameters. Previously, calling these methods from code that used `unsafe` blocks still required a project-level `<AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks>` setting because the attribute enforced that requirement independently. Now, only the standard `unsafe` block or method modifier is required.

Affected APIs include:

*   [Buffer.MemoryCopy](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.buffer.memorycopy)
*   [ReadOnlySpan<T>.ReadOnlySpan<T>(Void\*, Int32)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.readonlyspan-1.-ctor#system-readonlyspan-1-ctor\(system-void*-system-int32\)) and [Span<T>.Span<T>(Void\*, Int32)](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.span-1.-ctor#system-span-1-ctor\(system-void*-system-int32\))
*   [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.unsafe) pointer methods such as `AsRef`, `Read`, `Write`, and `Copy`
*   [System.Runtime.InteropServices.NativeMemory](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.nativememory) methods
*   [System.Text.Encoding](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.text.encoding) pointer overloads (all encoding classes)
*   [System.Numerics.Vector](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.numerics.vector) pointer-based `Load` and `Store` methods
*   Interop marshalling types in [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshalling](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.interopservices.marshalling)

This change reduces friction for advanced scenarios such as interop authoring, memory-mapped files, and low-level buffer manipulation, where unsafe context is already required by the calling code.

## Breaking Changes Affecting Your App in .NET 11

### 1. GZipStream "zero bytes = no data" check ❌ BROKEN

### 2. TAR archives with invalid checksums ❌ BROKEN

**Change:** `TarReader` now **validates header checksums** and throws `InvalidDataException` on mismatch.

- **Before (.NET 10):** Invalid checksums silently ignored.
- **After (.NET 11):** Throws `InvalidDataException`.

Your legacy hand-crafted archives with bad checksums will fail to read. **Fix:** Catch `InvalidDataException` and either fix the archives or implement a custom fallback parser.

[Details](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/compatibility/core-libraries/11/tar-checksum-validation)

---

### 3. ZipArchive.CreateAsync lazy loading ❌ BROKEN

**Change:** `CreateAsync` now **eagerly loads** all entries during the async call (no more deferred synchronous reads).

- **Before (.NET 10):** Entries loaded lazily on first `.Entries` access (synchronous I/O).
- **After (.NET 11):** All entries loaded during `await CreateAsync(...)`.

If you relied on lazy loading (e.g., deferring memory pressure, catching entry errors individually), that won't work anymore. Errors surface at `CreateAsync` time. **Fix:** Handle `InvalidDataException` at the `CreateAsync` call site and account for the higher memory usage at creation time.

[Details](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/compatibility/core-libraries/11/ziparchive-createasync-eager-load)

### 4. MemoryStream with very large allocations — ⚠️ No documented breaking change

I found **no .NET 11 breaking change** specific to `MemoryStream` maximum capacity. The `int.MaxValue` (~2 GB) limit still applies. This scenario should continue working as before, but keep an eye on the [full breaking changes list](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/compatibility/11) as .NET 11 is still in preview (currently Preview 5).
